A literature-informed read of the March 16, 2022 FOMC statement is mixed. The Committee acknowledges strong activity and job gains, but emphasizes elevated inflation driven by pandemic supply-demand imbalances and energy shocks, now exacerbated by Russia’s invasion of Ukraine—classic cost-push forces that worsen the output–inflation tradeoff. Standard policy rules (Taylor rule; Romer and Romer evidence on systematic responses) would imply meaningful tightening given low unemployment and high inflation, consistent with the 25 bp hike, guidance for “ongoing increases,” and planned balance sheet reduction. Forecast-based targeting insights (Svensson and Woodford, 2005) and New Keynesian Phillips Curve views stress anchoring expectations; however, energy-price shocks and supply-chain disruptions can transmit persistence. The statement’s nod to uncertainty aligns with “inflation-at-risk” perspectives—risks skewed to the upside—while Bullard’s dissent for a 50 bp move reflects a front-loading approach sometimes advocated when inflation pressures are broad-based. Although pandemic-era measurement issues (e.g., altered consumption weights) can affect CPI readings, the breadth of pressures and QT’s likely upward effect on term premia (QE/QT literature) point to tighter financial conditions ahead. Net tone: labor-market strength is positive, but inflation and geopolitical risks tilt sentiment slightly negative.
